The battle reports from Hexi have arrived. Are the commanders carrying out their orders? Suo Jing may be a quiet one, but he has a good head and his own judgment. When matters arise, consult with him more.
War is a matter of deception. You may judge and decide as the situation demands. There is only one thing. When you charge, keep your distance from the arrows. Bravery is admirable, but if the commander is lost, who will take responsibility for these hundred thousand sons of Hexi?
Hexi nights are always cold. Wear cotton in the evening and lighter clothes by day, and have your guards fasten the tent doors tightly. Make sure you eat your fill. If I hear again that you are eating less because there is lamb but no flatbread, then when you return, I will make you taste every bitter green in Guazhou.

I struck a deal with the general: I provide the grain, and he builds the well.
Even migrating birds need a place to rest on their long journey. For the Sogdian caravans, these resting places are always found where there is water.
But this time, my stay has been longer than I intended—perhaps because digging a well is a slow and arduous task.
At first, the Tang army sent only a few men. They still had a city to guard, so progress was slow. Just as I'd calculated, it was not a profitable deal.
But then, villagers started to appear. They helped the soldiers, not for coin or for profit. They couldn't quite explain why, only murmuring about wanting to see the Central Plains, to see Chang'an again.
Chang'an. I once longed for that city myself. In the lessons of trade passed down from my elders, it was a land one could only travel to after becoming a great merchant, carrying credentials and chanting prayers.
But what reason did these soldiers and villagers have, most of whom had never even been there?
I asked the general as he stood on the city wall. He told me Chang'an is the heart of their country. Their homeland.
I didn't understand what "homeland" meant. "A homeland," he explained, "is where you have ties. It's the place that lets a wanderer stop wandering."
His meaning still eluded me. "If I go to Chang'an myself," I asked, "will I understand?"
He shook his head. "You would. But you shouldn't go. Not now."
"If I would understand, then I must go." I smiled, countering with a new business proposal. "You've been looking for a foreigner the Bodchen wouldn't suspect, someone to travel light and carry a message to Chang'an. Let me go for you!"
I leaned forward, snatched the whip from his hand, and set off on his white horse, crossing three passes and a thousand miles to reach the fabled city of Chang'an.
It was magnificent. But strangely, I found myself missing the simple market where I'd spent my days with the soldiers and villagers.
When I returned, I saw a small light flickering in the shelter where I had stayed.
The guard at the gate greeted me with a smile. "The general said your return was uncertain, Master Kang, so he ordered us to keep a lamp lit for you."
In that moment, I understood. This is what a homeland is.
Suddenly, I had a new dream: to build this place bigger, better. To let the desert poplars sink their roots here and grow a thousand golden branches.
I want to build my "homeland" into a true home for the Sogdian people.

I have waited my entire life.
Waited until the Tang banner had been absent from this land for nearly sixty years.
People say a man knows his destiny by fifty. But what I awaited was not a destiny given by heaven.
So I fought against time itself, even if it meant betraying my kindness, abusing my power, and sacrificing... my own brother.
No, even if it meant sacrificing myself. Liangzhou can survive without me. The Guiyi Army can survive without me.
But the vow to return to our homeland demands a successor.
And today, I awaited that successor's arrival.

The man I wait for, however, still holds the passion of an idealist, and his respect for me.
A hostage in Chang'an cannot be the weakness of the Guiyi Army's leader.
So I showed him the truth, in all its glory and its filth.
I wanted him to forsake me, just as I forsook my brother.
If the transfer of power demands blood, then let my own flesh pave his way to greatness—
until he commands my old guard and his prestige surpasses my own.
I see his loyal soldiers outside. I see him silencing those who oppose our return to the Tang.
As expected, he has performed masterfully.

I thought he would come with a blade to my throat.
Instead, he offered the blade to me.
I know this blade. In our first parting, my brother gave it to me.
Later, I gave it to his son.
And now, it has returned to my hands.
He said he would lead the Guiyi Army, and wait for me to come home.
In that moment, we understood everything without a word. I know that now, and in the future, across a thousand miles or ten thousand, we will always stand by each other's side.

I took the register of names. And with it, his unspoken debt.
Patar taught me this was a fool's bargain, a trade destined for loss.
But he was wrong. In truth, I have been the one in debt all along—since five years past, ten, since the very first well was dug to bind Hexi together.
In the desert, a merchant follows water. Water draws people, and people are the source of all wealth.
Their wells became my trade routes. Their sacrifice gave me Poplar Bazaar.
It is time to settle my account.

This departure will be long. I wonder, will I see the poplars green again?
I must believe so. I believe in my own strength, and I believe in his vow.
"Sentiment is a weakness in our trade," my Patar used to say. But look how far it has brought me.
From Hexi to Chang'an, to Jingchu and beyond. My road is long yet.
And I know he, too, will keep walking his path, until the promise is fulfilled and the land is one.
